column2: to fall from favor, to lose one's standing and be cast aside ("to be put out to pasture")
column3: to have one's shoe thrown onto the roof
column4: In the Ahi organization and the guilds, a craftsman who produced defective goods or cheated a customer was judged under the supervision of the kethüda (guild warden) and the yiğitbaşı (guild steward). According to the account, the guilty master's shoe was thrown onto the roof of his shop so that everyone could see he had been expelled from the market. Since the shoe stood for the person himself, a shoe on the roof was a sign announcing that professional honor had been lost. Because this custom does not appear explicitly in the written fütüvvetnâmes, the explanation has the character of a folk account.

column2: to complete one's apprenticeship and journeymanship and rise to master status; to earn the right to set up one's own business
column3: to tie a peştemal (work apron) around one's waist
column4: In the guild system a journeyman (kalfa) passed to mastership with his master's approval, in a ceremony held in the presence of the kethüda. During the ceremony a peştemal was tied around the journeyman's waist by his master or in the name of the organization's pîr (patron saint); this sash certified that he could now open his own shop. This is the form that the şed-binding rite described in the fütüvvetnâmes took among tradesmen. The peştemal was a work apron but also a symbol of professional identity, which is why the idiom today denotes reaching full competence in a field.

column2: to be accepted as a full member of the Ahi organization or of a trade
column3: to tie a sash around one's waist
column4: In the Ahi tradition the şed is the sash symbolizing entry into a trade. As described in the fütüvvetnâmes, during the ceremony the şed was tied around the candidate's waist with three knots, and with each knot he was reminded of the binding of eye, tongue and loins: not to look at what is forbidden, not to speak ill and to guard one's honor. Peştemal kuşanmak is this ceremony transposed into the language of tradesmen. The expression appears in Ottoman guild records as the equivalent of a certificate of mastership.

column2: to begin work after receiving authority and permission from a master or an elder
column3: to take someone's hand; to take from someone's hand
column4: In the Ahi and dervish-order traditions, authority was transmitted from hand to hand. The master took his apprentice's hand and gave him permission to carry on the trade, and with this permission the apprentice was deemed to have received the hand. Hand-holding has been a sign of allegiance and contract since the age of the Kutadgu Bilig. Today it is used to state that one has received authority to do a job from an elder; its counterpart el vermek ("to give the hand") describes the party transferring the authority.

column2: to receive from a master a certificate authorizing one to teach an art or a body of knowledge
column3: to receive a permission document
column4: The word icazet, of Arabic origin, means permission. The teacher in the madrasa and the master in the calligrapher's workshop would give a student a written permission showing that he had reached a certain level. In calligraphy, the icazet meant the student could sign his own name for the first time. In the Ahi guilds, too, a journeyman had to receive an icazet from his master before he could open a shop. The expression lives on today in the sense of formal or informal approval.

column2: to finish one's apprenticeship and advance to the next rank; to reach adequate maturity in a job
column3: to come out of being an apprentice
column4: In the guild system the ranks of a trade were ordered as apprentice (çırak), journeyman (kalfa) and master (usta). The apprentice worked for years beside his master without pay or for low pay, and once he had learned the finer points of the craft he passed to journeymanship in a ceremony. This transition was called çırak çıkmak. Today the idiom describes shedding one's inexperience and becoming competent in a field; the parallel forms usta çıkmak and kalfa çıkmak have also been used.

column2: to reach the point of earning one's own living ("to stand on one's own two feet")
column3: for one's hand to be able to hold bread
column4: In the language of tradesmen, ekmek ("bread") is the name for a livelihood earned through labor. An apprentice beginning to receive a fixed wage, no longer being a burden on his family and being able to bring bread home, was described with this idiom. Since in Old Turkic el ("hand") also carried the sense of power and competence, a hand holding bread signals the maturing of both body and skill. Today the idiom is often used when speaking of children finding employment.

column2: the job or workplace that provides one's livelihood ("one's bread and butter")
column3: the door where bread is obtained
column4: In Ottoman society, attaching oneself to a door (kapı) meant entering the service of an employer or a notable. A tradesman's shop, a dervish lodge kitchen and a mansion's gate were all sources of livelihood in the same way. The phrase ekmek kapısı denotes the place to which a worker owes his living. For this reason, betraying one's ekmek kapısı was counted among the gravest faults in Ahi ethics. The expression remains in wide use today in the sense of workplace.

column2: to jeopardize someone's livelihood
column3: to play games with someone's bread
column4: In the guild system every master had a defined circle of customers and share of the work. Poaching another's customers, disparaging his work or undercutting his prices to spoil his market were serious offenses under Ahi custom; such people were warned by the kethüda and, if they persisted, were expelled from the market. Since bread was the concrete name for a livelihood, this behavior came to be called playing with someone's bread. Today the idiom describes undermining someone's job security.

column2: the tradesmen's common mutual-aid fund
column3: the common chest
column4: In the Ottoman guilds every trade community had a common fund. Members' dues, the fees paid by those passing to mastership and donations accumulated in this chest. From it, aid was given to the families of tradesmen who fell ill, went bankrupt or died, and when necessary capital was advanced to apprentices. The chest was under the supervision of the kethüda and the yiğitbaşı. The expression was later used for mutual-aid funds of every kind.

column2: a phrase expressing good wishes to someone at work
column3: may the work come easy
column4: This wish, addressed to a tradesman whose shop one enters, to a laborer in the field or to a master busy at his forge, is connected with the work ethic of the Ahi tradition. Respecting labor and wishing that a task end well was a rule of courtesy among tradesmen. The phrase is in the optative mood; the reply was sağ ol ("thank you") or hoş geldin ("welcome"). Today it is one of the most common greeting formulas in Turkish.

column2: a phrase of thanks and blessing said by a tradesman to a customer after a sale
column3: may God grant abundance
column4: In Ahi ethics what mattered was not the size of one's earnings but their blessedness. On taking the money, the tradesman closed the transaction with a prayer, wishing abundance for the customer's goods and for his own earnings. The word bereket, of Arabic origin, means increase, abundance and good fortune. The phrase springs from the same outlook as the siftah prayer said at the first sale of the morning. It is still used today in place of thanks in monetary transactions.

column2: a wish said by a tradesman to the customer who makes the first sale of the day
column3: the first sale from you, abundance from God
column4: Siftah, from the Arabic root of iftitah ("opening"), is the first transaction of the day. The tradesman regarded the first sale as auspicious and would touch the money to his counter or his face, wishing for abundance throughout the day. In the Ahi outlook, a tradesman who had made his siftah would send customers to a neighbor who had not yet made his. The set phrase sums up the belief in the good luck of the first customer and in God as the true owner of all earnings. It is still heard every morning in the marketplace.

column2: having a trade will support a person under any circumstances
column3: a craft is like a golden bracelet
column4: The proverb says that a craft, like a bracelet on one's arm, goes everywhere with its owner and can be cashed in to provide a living when needed. In Ottoman society the gold bracelet was a woman's security and a craft was a man's. The importance the Ahi tradition attached to acquiring a trade is summed up in this saying. It is still used today when advising children to learn a trade.

column2: every task belongs to the one who knows it and dares to do it
column3: work belongs to the one who knows it, the sword to the one who girds it
column4: The proverb places two separate social spheres side by side: a craft should be left to its expert, and a weapon to the one entitled to carry it. In the Ahi system a person who did not know a trade was forbidden to open a shop; in military life, too, bearing a sword was the right of a particular class. The saying makes the idea of merit concrete through these two examples. Its structure, an elliptical sentence built on possessive endings, preserves an archaic proverb form.

column2: a highly experienced person who knows a job better than anyone
column3: the founder, the venerable elder of the trade
column4: The Persian pîr means old and venerable. In the fütüvvet tradition every trade was held to have a spiritual founder: Idris for tailors, Adam for farmers, Ahi Evran for saddlers, and so on. These pîrs were commemorated in tradesmen's prayers and guild ceremonies. Over time, anyone who knew a job exceptionally well also came to be called the pîr of that trade. The expression is used today as praise for mastery and experience.

column2: work done with care and skill ("a professional job")
column3: work from a master's hand
column4: In the guild system only someone who had received a certificate of mastership could sell products under his own name. Work done by apprentices and journeymen was not handed to customers without passing the master's inspection, and if a defective product was found the master was held responsible. For this reason the phrase usta işi came to mean a guarantee of quality. Its opposites, çırak işi ("apprentice work") and acemi işi ("novice work"), denote careless products. The expression is still used as praise today.

column2: to give up resisting and submit; to withdraw one's claim ("to strike one's colors")
column3: to lower the sails until they touch the water
column4: On a sailing ship the sign of resistance is the sails filled with wind. In battle or pursuit, a ship that lowered its sails lost speed and signaled its surrender. In the galley age, lowering the sails completely meant abandoning one's fighting strength. The idiom was born of this signal of surrender and over time came to describe backing down in an argument or a negotiation. The form yelkenleri indirmek is used in the same sense.

column2: to capsize, to be turned upside down; for matters to go completely wrong
column3: for a boat to turn over
column4: Alabora is a term that passed from Italian seafaring language into Ottoman seamanship; the word, which described raising a sail or yard up toward the mast, shifted to mean overturning along with the boat. The levends (marines) and reis (captains) Turkified many words from the common Mediterranean seafarers' language in this way. A boat turning over means everything at sea vanishing in an instant, which is why the idiom is used for any situation whose order collapses.

column2: to change direction; to change one's attitude abruptly
column3: to turn the rudder hard to one side
column4: Dümen ("rudder") passed into Turkish from Italian timone. To change a ship's heading the tiller is turned sharply to one side; sailors call this dümen kırmak. Pîrî Reis's Kitâb-ı Bahriye describes in detail the points along the coasts where course changes are made. The idiom passed from the language of ships into that of politics and daily life, coming to describe a person changing opinion or course.

column2: to labor at something that will yield no result ("to flog a dead horse")
column3: to swing the oars without moving the boat forward
column4: The oar was the basic power of the galley age; galley slaves and oarsmen rowed for hours at the same tempo. In a boat that could not make headway against current or wind, the oars were pulled with great effort yet did not budge the vessel. Sailors called this boşa kürek çekmek. Today the idiom is used for any situation in which effort goes unrewarded; the word kürek ("oar") occurs with the same meaning in Old Turkic.

column2: to settle in a place and stay a long time
column3: to drop a ship's anchor into the water
column4: In the language of Ottoman sailors the anchor was called demir ("iron"). A ship entering harbor dropped its anchor to hold position against the current, and weighed anchor (demir almak) on departure. In the Kitâb-ı Bahriye, Pîrî Reis records one by one the bays in which to anchor. The idiom passed from ship language into everyday speech, coming to describe settling in somewhere, especially overstaying as a guest. Demir almak, by contrast, signals setting out.

column2: at full speed and without meeting any obstacle ("full sail ahead")
column3: a sail filled by wind from the stern
column4: Pupa, from Italian poppa, is a nautical term for the stern of a ship. A wind blowing directly from astern drives a sailing vessel most comfortably; sailors call this pupa yelken gitmek ("to sail with a following wind"). On Ottoman galleons a wind from astern meant a shorter voyage. The expression is used today for a task proceeding smoothly and fast.

column2: to stray from the path one should follow; to not know what to do ("to lose one's bearings")
column3: for a ship to lose the course it should follow
column4: Rota ("course") passed into Turkish from Italian rotta and is the line a ship follows on the chart. Because finding one's way on the open sea without compass and chart was hard, captains like Pîrî Reis drew coastal charts in great detail. A ship that lost its course could run onto rocks or into the enemy. Borrowed from ship language, the idiom is used for a person or institution that has lost sight of its goal.

column2: to be at a loss as to what to do ("to lose one's bearings")
column3: to lose the direction shown by the compass
column4: Pusula ("compass") comes from Italian bussola and has been used on Ottoman ships since the fifteenth century. A captain unable to read his compass in a storm or in fog could not find the ship's heading. Pîrî Reis describes the use of the compass and navigation by the stars in the Kitâb-ı Bahriye. The idiom expresses bewilderment and indecision as the everyday counterpart of losing one's heading.

column2: to be side by side, very close; to come close enough to clash
column3: for the sides of two ships to touch
column4: Borda, from Italian bordo, is the term for the side of a ship. In galley battles, after the exchange of cannon fire the ships drew alongside one another and the levends leapt onto the ships that had come broadside to broadside to join in sword fighting. This form of close combat was the decisive moment of great naval battles such as Lepanto. The expression is used today for two parties confronting each other at very close quarters.

column2: worthless, insignificant, good for nothing
column3: with a broken stern (or rear end)
column4: In ship language kıç is the stern section of a vessel. According to the account, boats whose stern was broken could not put to sea and were left to rot on the shore, which is why useless things came to be called kıçı kırık. Some hold that the phrase arose from a coarse comparison with the body. Since no written record exists, the nautical origin is passed on as a folk account. The idiom is used to express contempt.

column2: for a project to grind to a halt, to become stuck ("to run aground")
column3: for a ship to touch bottom in shallow water and get stuck
column4: A ship driven toward the shore in shallow water or in a storm settles on the bottom and cannot free itself under its own power. In the Kitâb-ı Bahriye, shoals and reefs are carefully marked against this danger. A grounded ship could not be refloated without unloading its cargo, and most often broke apart. Borrowed from ship language, the idiom is used to express that an undertaking can no longer progress.

column2: to follow in someone's footsteps, to do whatever he says ("to follow in someone's wake")
column3: to proceed along the trail left by the rudder of the ship ahead
column4: The rudder of a moving ship leaves a foamy trail behind it; sailors call this dümen suyu ("wake"). Galleys setting out as a fleet proceeded in formation in the wake of the flagship, so that they both found their way and kept order. The idiom passed from ship language into everyday speech to describe a person who follows a superior without making his own decisions. It is mostly used in a critical tone.

column2: to engage in tricks and intrigue, to secretly serve one's own interest
column3: to turn the rudder
column4: The rudder is the instrument that sets a ship's direction, and no one but the helmsman may touch it. Turned in a place the passengers cannot see, the rudder silently changes the ship's course. This secrecy carried the word into slang: in nineteenth-century Istanbul slang dümen acquired the sense of trick and ruse. Dümen çevirmek thus means to cheat, and dümenci means a trickster.

column2: to set out on a voyage or embark on a new venture ("to set sail")
column3: to spread the sails to the wind
column4: A ship leaving harbor first weighs anchor, then opens its sails to catch the wind. This is the moment the voyage truly begins. The Ottoman navy set sail in spring and returned to the arsenal in autumn. The word yelken ("sail") comes from the Old Turkic root yel ("wind"). The idiom has carried the excitement of putting out to sea over to every kind of new beginning and has been used especially often in poetic language.

column2: everyone looks after his own affairs and interests ("every man for himself")
column3: whoever saves his ship counts as captain
column4: In a storm or a battle every captain thinks first of his own ship; at the moment the fleet scattered, a captain who brought his ship safely to port was deemed to have done his duty. Kaptan passed into Ottoman seafaring from Italian capitano. The idiom generalizes this principle to describe situations in which everyone tries only to save his own skin. It is mostly said to criticize selfishness.

column2: to cut off any way back, to commit irrevocably ("to burn one's boats")
column3: to set the ships on fire
column4: According to the account, Tariq ibn Ziyad, commander of the Muslim army that landed in Spain, had the ships burned so that his soldiers would not think of turning back. The same story is told of the Spanish commander Cortés on reaching America. The historicity of these events is disputed among historians, but because the story is widespread the idiom has entered many languages. In Turkish it denotes making a decision from which there is no return.

column2: goods sold very cheaply, far below their value ("fire-sale goods")
column3: cargo salvaged from a sunken ship
column4: The salvaged cargo of ships that had run ashore or sunk was considered soaked and spoiled and was disposed of quickly at very low prices. In Ottoman port cities the auction of such goods was a routine event. Street vendors would cry batan geminin malları to announce a bargain. Today the idiom is said of things sold absurdly cheap or squandered as if worthless.

column2: a person in desperate straits hopes for help even from what may harm him ("a drowning man will clutch at a straw")
column3: one who falls into the sea clings even to a snake
column4: A person about to drown grabs whatever comes to hand and will not let go even if it is a snake. The proverb says that desperation drives people to dangerous options. In Ottoman society the sea was a source of both livelihood and death, and shipwrecks were everyday events. The saying is recorded in this same form in the era of the Kamus-ı Türkî and is still widely used to describe hopeless situations.

column2: a highly experienced sailor who knows the sea in all its moods ("an old sea dog")
column3: wolf of the sea
column4: In Turkish kurt ("wolf") is used for a master and veteran of a trade, as in işin kurdu olmak ("to be the wolf of the job"). In Ottoman seafaring the comparison was made for reis and levends who spent their years on galleys. The word kurt occurs in Old Turkic alongside börü and carries connotations of wisdom. The expression deniz kurdu is said respectfully today of old and experienced captains.

column2: a phrase said when beginning a task in God's name
column3: heave, in the name of God
column4: Vira, from Italian virare, is the command to begin hauling the anchor or a rope; mayna is its opposite. Ottoman sailors began turning the capstan to weigh anchor by saying bismillah, and so the two words fused. These command words passed into Turkish from the common Mediterranean seafarers' language. The set phrase is used today, in jest or in earnest, when starting any kind of task.

column2: to keep one's distance from a matter or a person without getting involved
column3: to anchor offshore, away from the coast
column4: Alarga comes from Italian allargare and describes a ship moving away from the shore. Ships that did not come into harbor or were waiting their turn anchored offshore, at alarga. The word was among the everyday commands of Ottoman sailors. The idiom expresses staying out of an argument or a matter as the everyday counterpart of waiting offshore. The form alarga etmek is also used.

column2: for something to have begun irreversibly ("the die is cast")
column3: for the arrow to have shot from the bow
column4: An arrow that has left the bow cannot be recalled; this observation is one of the oldest lessons of archery. Turkish archery was the foundation of both war and the hunt from Central Asia onward, and the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk contains a great many words relating to the bow and arrow. The idiom states that a process without return has begun. The same observation echoes in proverbs saying that a word once spoken cannot be taken back.

column2: to score a direct hit, to achieve exactly the right result ("to hit the bull's-eye")
column3: to hit the twelve-point center of the target
column4: On target boards the central ring gives the highest score, and in traditional Turkish marksmanship this ring counted as twelve. In the puta (target) shooting of Ottoman archers, too, hitting the center of the target brought the highest praise. On ikiden vurmak means a direct hit on the center. The idiom passed from the language of marksmanship into everyday speech to say that a remark or a decision has hit the mark exactly.

column2: to become very angry, to stiffen with rage
column3: to tense up like a drawn bow
column4: Before an arrow is shot the bowstring is drawn and the bow is strained with all its force; at this moment the bow is at its tautest and most dangerous. Ottoman archers called this state of the bow kiriş çekmek ("drawing the string"). The tensing of an angry person's muscles has been likened to this tension. The idiom describes at once the stiffening of the body and anger ready to burst.

column2: to make headway, to cover a distance
column3: to reach a menzil (stage, range)
column4: The Arabic menzil means a halting place and a distance to be reached. In Ottoman archery menzil means the farthest point an arrow reaches; a menzil stone was erected where the arrow of a record-breaking archer fell at the Okmeydanı. On caravan and post roads every halting station was also called a menzil. The idiom draws on both usages to express covering a distance.

column2: to do harm and then evade responsibility, to hide one's guilt
column3: to hide the bow after shooting the arrow
column4: Whose bow an arrow had come from could be told from the bowstring and the length of the arrow. An archer who hides his bow is trying to erase the trail of the arrow he shot. The idiom presents this behavior as an example of slyness: to do harm and then appear innocent. Within the rule-bound structure of Ottoman archery such conduct was counted a great disgrace. The saying is used in an insinuating, reproachful tone.

column2: to spring into motion suddenly and very fast ("to shoot off like an arrow")
column3: to dart off with the speed of an arrow leaving the bow
column4: The composite bow used by Ottoman archers hurled the arrow very far and at great speed; in distance shooting, records exceeding eight hundred meters are known. The sudden speed of the arrow at the moment it leaves the bow became a measure of speed in Turkish. The idiom is used for a person who leaps up from where he is sitting and runs; the form yerinden ok gibi fırlamak is also common.

column2: to run away, to slip off ("to make a break for it")
column3: to break the bowstring
column4: The kiriş is the cord of sinew or gut that strings the bow and launches the arrow. A bow whose string has snapped is useless; a person who wished to withdraw from battle or a contest was deemed to have broken his string. Whether the idiom comes from this sense of kiriş or from running so hard as to strain the body's tendons (also kiriş) is not certain. Today, in a slangy tone, it describes fleeing a place in haste.

column2: a deed once done or a word once spoken cannot be undone
column3: an arrow shot from the bow does not return to it
column4: The proverb turns archery's most basic observation into a principle of life. In Turkish archery, because the arrow did not return to its owner once shot, archers weighed every shot. The testing of heroes with bow and arrow in the Dede Korkut tales shows the antiquity of this culture. The saying is used to recall the consequences of decisions taken and promises made without thought.

column2: to be the object of everyone's attacks, criticism or mockery ("to be a sitting target")
column3: to be the board that is aimed at
column4: In Ottoman marksmanship, targets called puta, made of leather or wood, were set up at the Okmeydanı and the archers shot at them in turn. The target board took hundreds of arrows without ever answering back. The expression likens this passive condition to a person who is constantly criticized. Hedef ("target") is a word of Arabic origin; forms built with tahta ("board") or nişan ("mark") are also used today.

column2: to be an excellent marksman; to succeed in every attempt
column3: to hit everything one aims at
column4: In hunting and archery the measure of mastery is that every shot finds its target. In the Ottoman hunting establishment, the falconers and archers who went hunting with the sultan were praised in these terms. Taken from the language of marksmanship, the idiom came to be used for a person who succeeds at everything he undertakes. Because atmak ("to shoot") has been used since Old Turkic for both arrows and bullets, the idiom has lived through both eras.

column2: to let no one pass or escape ("to keep an airtight watch")
column3: to not let even a bird fly past
column4: At the frontier posts and on the castle towers where falconers and archers served, every movement was watched. Surveillance so tight that not even a bird could pass was described as kuş uçurtmamak. In Ottoman hunting, kuş uçurmak meant releasing a trained falcon at its prey, and this phrase too may have played a part in the idiom's formation. The idiom survives today in the sense of strict control and close guarding.

column2: whoever seeks to harm another may be harmed himself ("the hunter becomes the hunted")
column3: the one who goes hunting may be hunted
column4: Hunting was both a livelihood and training for war in Turkish culture. A person who went hunting in the forest might meet a bear or a wolf and become prey rather than hunter. The proverb speaks this truth as a warning to anyone trying to trap another. The saying carries the cultural background of the hunting scenes in the Dede Korkut tales, with the same meaning, and is still widely used.

column1: avcı ne kadar hile bilse ayı o kadar yol bilir
column2: however cunning one may be, the other side also knows its own ways
column3: however many tricks the hunter knows, the bear knows that many escape routes
column4: Bear hunting in Anatolia was a dangerous business requiring long preparation; hunters set traps and lay in wait. But the bear, too, knew the forest well and fled by paths the hunter could not see. The proverb counsels against underestimating the other side. It draws a social lesson from a hunter's observation and is said today in trade or politics to note that a rival is also prepared.

column2: to lie hidden in wait to attack or capture someone ("to set an ambush")
column3: to prepare a hiding place
column4: A pusu is the place where a hunter hides to wait for game. The word, derived from the Turkish root pus-, is also used in the era of the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk. Hunters set ambushes by the waterside or at passes and waited for game such as partridge and deer. The same method was applied in war. The idiom denotes secretly watching for an opportunity and also survives in the forms pusuya düşmek ("to fall into an ambush") and pusuya yatmak ("to lie in ambush").

column2: to incite both sides at once and act two-facedly ("to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds")
column3: to say "run" to the hare and "catch" to the hound
column4: Hare hunting with hounds (tazı) was among the most common forms of Ottoman hunting. The hunter loosed the hound on the hare and watched the animal's flight. A person who tells the hare to run and the hound to catch it is a hypocrite inciting both sides. The idiom draws a social criticism from this hunting scene and is said of two-faced mediators. In Turkish, tazı is the name of a hunting dog used since Old Turkic.

column2: aiming carefully; heading straight for the target
column3: to bring the notch, the eye and the bead into line
column4: Gez is the notch of the arrow that sits on the bowstring and the rear sight of a rifle; the arpacık is the small projection at the end of the barrel. When aiming, the eye, the notch and the bead are brought into a single line. The word gez, inherited from Ottoman archery, was carried over into the era of firearms. The expression passed into everyday speech as a summary of the marksman's lesson and came to describe doing a job with one's aim fixed squarely on the target.

column2: to endure great hardship and suffering
column3: to complete a forty-day period of seclusion
column4: The Persian word çihil means forty; the çile is the period during which a dervish entering an order spent forty days in a closed cell, eating and sleeping little. In the Mevlevî lodge this period lasted a thousand and one days, during which the dervish matured by serving in the kitchen. Because the çile period was a hard trial, the word began to describe hardship of every kind. Today the idiom has moved away from its Sufi meaning and simply denotes enduring torment.

column2: a struggle to gain position and office ("a turf war")
column3: a fight over the sheikh's sheepskin seat
column4: In the dervish lodges, the sheepskin or wolfskin (post) on which the sheikh sat was the symbol of his office. When a sheikh died, who would succeed him became a matter of dispute, and at times long disagreements arose among his deputies. These struggles were called post kavgası. The expression passed from lodge language into politics and business to describe any struggle for office. Posta oturmak means to assume a position.

column2: to vanish, to leave without a trace ("to vanish into thin air")
column3: to set foot on the secret, to step into concealment
column4: The Arabic kadem means foot and sır means hidden knowledge. In Sufism it was believed that certain saints disappeared from sight and hid themselves without dying; figures like Hızır appear suddenly and vanish suddenly in the tales. Such persons were said to have set foot on the secret. The idiom passed from this belief into everyday speech and today describes a person suddenly disappearing. It is mostly used in a playful tone.

column2: to grant authority and permission to a student or disciple
column3: to extend one's hand and have it held
column4: In the dervish orders the sheikh conferred the authority of spiritual guidance on his deputy during a ceremony by having him hold his hand. The root of this tradition is the ceremony of allegiance (biat); holding hands signifies a pledge of loyalty. In the Ahi guilds, too, the master gave his hand to the apprentice, granting him permission to carry on the trade. Today the idiom denotes an elder giving his approval. El almak signals the other direction, that is, the party receiving the authority.

column2: to suppress one's desires, to rein in one's appetites
column3: to blunt the self (nefs)
column4: The Arabic nefs is, in Sufism, the source of a person's selfish wishes and desires. The dervish's path is to mature by disciplining his nefs; eating little, sleeping little and speaking little are parts of this training. Blunting the nefs means lessening the sharpness of one's desires. In everyday speech the idiom is often used in a softened sense, such as taking the edge off one's hunger.

column2: to lose oneself in rapture, joy or a faint ("to be carried away")
column3: to go out of one's own self
column4: In Sufism, vecd (ecstasy) is the dervish forgetting his self and turning toward God during zikr or sema. The dervish whirling in the Mevlevî sema loses himself to the point of forgetting his surroundings. This state was rendered into Turkish as kendinden geçmek. The idea of transcending the self is treated often in the poems of Yunus Emre. Today the idiom is used to describe both rapture and fainting.

column2: to be carried away with enthusiasm, to spring into action with great zeal
column3: to enter the state of love (aşk)
column4: In Sufism, aşk is the ecstatic state of love for God. During zikr and sema the dervish comes into aşk, and his body and tongue move with this rapture. In Bektaşî and Mevlevî gatherings it was said of a dervish reciting a nefes (hymn) that he had come into aşk. Today the idiom describes enthusiasm of every kind, even, in jest, warming to a task. The word aşk is Arabic and has been established in Turkish since the time of Yunus Emre.

column2: to assume an office, to take over leadership
column3: to sit on the sheikh's sheepskin seat
column4: In the lodge the sheikh sat on the sheepskin (post) spread before the mihrab; this post was the sign of his spiritual office. A new sheikh sat on the post in a ceremony and the dervishes declared their allegiance to him. In the Mevlevî order this ceremony was confirmed by the Çelebi in Konya. The idiom passed from lodge language into politics, coming to describe acceding to an office. Post kavgası and postu sermek are other idioms from the same root.

column2: to become furious, to run out of patience ("to lose one's temper")
column3: to leave the çile cell
column4: The çile is the forty-day period of secluded devotion and patience kept by a dervish. A dervish who could not complete this period and left the cell was deemed to have failed the test. Çileden çıkmak thus began to describe the exhaustion of patience. The idiom has lost its Sufi meaning and today denotes only losing oneself in anger. The word çile comes from the Persian çihil, meaning forty.

column2: to face death rather than reveal a secret
column3: to give one's head but not one's secret
column4: The Persian ser means head. In Sufism the knowledge a spiritual guide disclosed to his disciple was counted a secret and was not spoken outside. The stories of Sufis such as Hallâc-ı Mansûr, executed for revealing the secret, reinforced this principle. Built on the sound-alike words ser and sır, the idiom expresses the highest degree of loyalty. Today it is said of trustworthy people who keep secrets.

column2: an immature, coarse and uncouth person
column3: unripe souls
column4: The Arabic ervah is the plural of ruh ("soul"). In Sufism the human soul matures by passing through the çile and through training; the soul of a person who did not walk this path was considered raw. Mevlânâ's metaphor of cooking and burning is a product of the same outlook. Used in lodge language for coarse people, the expression passed into everyday speech with the meaning of uncouth. In Turkish, ham is the same word for unripe fruit and for an unripe soul.

column2: to reach maturity, to attain the most accomplished state
column3: to arrive at completeness
column4: The Arabic kemal means completeness and maturity. In Sufism a person's aim is to become the perfect human (insan-ı kâmil) by disciplining the nefs; the dervish who advances on this path reaches kemal. From the Kutadgu Bilig onward, the concept of maturity is mentioned together with virtue in Turkish texts. Today the idiom is used both for personal maturity and for the full development of a work. The words kâmil and kemalat come from the same root.

column2: to pledge oneself to a path or a dervish order
column3: to declare one's acceptance openly
column4: The Arabic ikrar is the open acknowledgment of something. In the Alevî-Bektaşî tradition a person entering the path gives ikrar at the cem ceremony before the dede and the community, promising to abide by the rules of the path. One who broke his ikrar was deemed düşkün (fallen) and was cast out of the community. The expression has also been used in legal language in the sense of confession. Today it survives in the sense of giving a firm promise.

column2: to mend one's ways, to return to proper behavior ("to come around")
column3: to come onto the right path
column4: In Sufism the very word tarikat means path; yola girmek ("to enter the path") is to attach oneself to a guide, and yoldan çıkmak ("to leave the path") is to break the rules. In the Alevî-Bektaşî tradition yol ("the path") is the name for the entire body of rules. Yola gelmek describes adopting the rules and reforming. In everyday speech the idiom is used of a child or a stubborn person. Tracing its origin to Sufism is one possible interpretation; the word yol also carries the sense of right conduct in Old Turkic.

column2: to settle somewhere and stay a long time ("to park oneself")
column3: to spread one's sheepskin on the ground in order to sit
column4: A dervish spread his sheepskin (post) wherever he went, sat on it and stayed there; the post was both his bed and his seat of office. A wandering dervish's stay at a lodge began with the spreading of his post. The idiom arose from this habit and in everyday speech, usually in a critical tone, came to describe staying somewhere longer than necessary. Posta oturmak, by contrast, is a separate idiom meaning to assume an office.

column1: dervişin fikri neyse zikri de odur
column2: whatever is in a person's mind is what comes out of his mouth
column3: whatever the dervish's thought is, that is what comes to his tongue
column4: Zikr is the words the dervish repeats to remember God. A true dervish reflects what is in his mind on his tongue; the zikr of a person whose mind is on worldly affairs drifts in that direction. The proverb says that a person's speech betrays his thinking. Built on the rhyme of fikir ("thought") and zikir ("remembrance"), the saying is one of the lasting traces that lodge culture has left on everyday language.

column2: to be content with little and set no store by worldly goods
column3: one morsel of food and one cloak to wear
column4: The hırka is the woolen cloak worn by a dervish; the word sufi is thought to be connected with suf, meaning wool. In Sufism, contentment is the condition for not being attached to the world: a morsel to fill the stomach and a cloak to cover the back are enough. The set phrase is the summary of this outlook. Today it is used both as praise and as a criticism directed at those seeking an excuse for idleness.

column2: without expecting anything in return, purely for love
column3: for the love of the pîr
column4: In the lodge and guild traditions every path has a pîr: Mevlânâ for the Mevlevîs, Hacı Bektaş Veli for the Bektaşîs. Dervishes took on hard tasks by saying they did them for love of the pîr. The set phrase passed from this spirit of voluntary service into everyday speech. Today it is said, often half in jest, of work done for nothing in return: pir aşkına yapıldı ("it was done for the love of the pîr").

column2: to show deep respect to a great person, to take refuge with him
column3: to touch one's face to the threshold of a door
column4: On entering a lodge one did not step on the threshold but bowed and kissed it; the threshold was the boundary of the sacred space. In the Mevlevî lodge, rubbing one's face on the threshold was the sign of devotion to the pîr. In Divan poetry, rubbing one's face on the threshold of the beloved or the sultan is the highest expression of servitude. Today the idiom denotes begging help from a great person or showing him respect. The word eşik ("threshold") has been used since Old Turkic.

column2: one who waits patiently at a task is rewarded in the end
column3: the one who serves at the lodge drinks the lodge's soup
column4: Soup was cooked every day in the lodge kitchens and distributed to dervishes and the poor alike. In the Mevlevî lodge, service in the kitchen was the new dervish's first training. A dervish who did not neglect his service both filled his stomach and advanced on his path. Starting from this arrangement, the proverb says that patiently staying in one place brings its reward. Today it is said of the rewards of loyalty in working life.

column2: to disappear, to become invisible ("to vanish into thin air")
column3: to join the company of the Forty
column4: Sufi belief holds that there are forty saints who secretly govern the world; they are called the Forty (kırklar). The Assembly of the Forty occupies an important place in Alevî-Bektaşî narratives. Since these saints were believed to be invisible to the eye, a person who suddenly disappeared was said to have joined the Forty. The idiom passed from the language of belief into everyday speech to describe someone vanishing without a trace.

column2: to rise in revolt, to rebel collectively ("to mutiny")
column3: to lift the cooking cauldron from its place
column4: In the janissary corps every orta (company) had a great cauldron, and this cauldron was the symbol of the unit; food distribution, meetings and oaths took place around it. When the janissaries were discontented they overturned the cauldron and carried it to the Et Meydanı, an open signal of rebellion against the sultan. Lifting the cauldron occurred many times until the corps was abolished in 1826. Today the idiom denotes collective revolt of every kind.

column2: to destroy someone's home, family or order of life
column3: to plant a fig tree where someone's hearth stood
column4: The roots of the fig tree split stone walls and the tree springs up of its own accord in ruined places; seeing a fig tree in ruins is a sign of destruction in Anatolia. In janissary language ocak ("hearth") is the name for both the unit and the family. A fig growing where a hearth once stood shows that the place has been wholly abandoned. The idiom arose from this observation and describes destroying someone's order of life. The form ocağına incir dikmek is also used.

column2: to take action for a cause, to rebel openly ("to raise the standard")
column3: to unfurl and fly the banner
column4: In the Ottoman state, when a campaign was decided the banners were unfurled and soldiers were summoned under the flag to assemble. Opening the flag was the signal both for the start of a campaign and for recruiting volunteers. A bey who opened a flag in a province was deemed to have risen against the center. The idiom is the everyday counterpart of this military tradition; it denotes openly taking up the struggle for an idea or a cause.

column2: to kill a community wholesale, to massacre ("to put to the sword")
column3: to pass everyone under the sword
column4: In siege warfare, putting to the sword a garrison that resisted and would not surrender was a common practice in both Ottoman and European laws of war. The verb geçirmek ("to pass through") in the idiom describes the sword passing over an entire community. The phrase occurs frequently in the Dede Korkut tales and in Ottoman chronicles. Today it is used in its literal sense for historical events and figuratively for harsh purges.

column2: to take over a group by winning one of its own members
column3: to capture the fortress from within
column4: In sieges, the easiest route to conquest was having a gate opened from inside rather than scaling the fortress walls. Ottoman siege history includes fortresses taken with help from within, and these events were recounted among the people. The idiom describes taking over a group by persuading one of its members rather than forcing it from outside. Today it is used often in politics and in business.

column2: very solid, unshakable, dependable ("solid as a rock")
column3: as solid as a fortress
column4: Kale, of Arabic origin, is a defensive structure surrounded by walls. On the Ottoman frontiers fortresses secured a region, and the fall of a fortress meant the loss of the whole region. For this reason the fortress was used as a measure of solidity. The expression is said today of sturdy structures, teams that play strong defense, or dependable people. The forms kale gibi durmak ("to stand like a fortress") and kale gibi adam ("a man like a fortress") are common.

column2: making it known to everyone, noisily ("with great fanfare")
column3: with drum and zurna playing
column4: The Mehterhane was the official band of the Ottoman army; declarations of campaign, victories and the sultan's processions were announced with drum and zurna. The same instruments were played at weddings and festivals in village squares. Because the sound of drum and zurna carried far, the impossibility of keeping an event secret was expressed with this phrase. Today the idiom describes doing something openly for all to see, mostly in a critical tone.

column2: to proclaim the decision to go on campaign, to prepare for war
column3: to plant a horsetail standard in the ground
column4: The tuğ is an ancient Turkic standard made of horsetail hair bound to a pole; it has been a symbol of khanly rule since the era of the Orkhon Inscriptions. In the Ottoman state, when the sultan decided on a campaign, tuğs were planted in front of the palace, and this signal meant the army was to assemble. The number of tuğs showed rank: viziers had three, the sultan seven. The expression occurs in historical texts as the symbol of preparation for campaign.

column2: to prepare for war; to ratify a sultan's accession by ceremony
column3: to gird a sword at one's waist
column4: After ascending the throne, Ottoman sultans girded the sword in a ceremony held at Eyüp Sultan; this ceremony corresponded to the coronation in Europe. In military usage, girding the sword means preparing for war. The verb kuşanmak is related to kuşak ("sash"), which derives from the Old Turkic word kur. The expression lived in both palace and army language and was used in proverbs as a measure of valor.

column2: making no progress in a task, constant stalling ("two steps forward, one step back")
column3: two steps forward, one step back
column4: According to the account, the mehter band, while marching, took two steps forward and one step back, saluting to right and left. This manner of marching conveys the mehter's slow tempo and pageantry. The idiom, drawing on this march, has been used for tasks that make no progress. However, since the claim that the mehter marched this way cannot be firmly confirmed by historical documents, the explanation has the character of a folk account.

column2: a tense situation or person ready to explode at any moment ("a powder keg")
column3: a barrel full of gunpowder
column4: In the Ottoman army gunpowder was transported in barrels for cannon and muskets and stored in special magazines in fortresses. Since a single spark could blow up an entire arsenal, a powder keg meant constant danger. Taken from this military reality, the expression has been used for tense people and regions on the brink of conflict. The word barut entered Turkish by way of Persian.

column2: a survivor of a massacre or a disaster
column3: what is left over from the sword
column4: The expression, used for those who were left behind and not killed in battle or massacre, belongs to the same world as the idiom kılıçtan geçirmek. In Ottoman chronicles, those who remained alive after the fall of a fortress were called kılıç artığı. Today the expression is used to describe survivors of a disaster; in slang it has also acquired a disparaging sense. The word artık ("leftover") comes from the Old Turkic root art-.

column2: to take a stand against a person or an idea
column3: to take up a position on the battle line
column4: Cephe, of Arabic origin, means the front face of a building and the line where an army meets the enemy. A soldier taking his place at the front means accepting battle with the other side. The idiom, built on the word cephe that became widespread in the wars of the late Ottoman period, denotes openly taking a stand against someone. The forms cephe açmak ("to open a front") and cephe oluşturmak ("to form a front") are also used.

column2: to oppose someone openly, to challenge to a fight or a contest ("to throw down the gauntlet")
column3: to call out loudly in the open field
column4: In ancient warfare, before two armies engaged, warriors came out onto the field and called for a champion from the other side, challenging him to single combat. Such scenes of challenge appear in the Dede Korkut tales and in Ottoman chronicles. The word okumak means to call in Old Turkic; meydan okumak means to call out on the field. Today the idiom denotes any kind of open defiance.

column2: to surrender, to admit defeat ("to raise the white flag")
column3: to hoist the white flag on the mast
column4: In war the white flag, as a sign of truce and surrender, entered the international rules of war from the European armies in the nineteenth century. The Ottoman army also adopted this signal. White conveys being undyed and flagless, that is, representing no state. Today the idiom is used to describe giving up in any kind of dispute. The form teslim bayrağını çekmek ("to hoist the flag of surrender") is also common.

column2: a person who has learned a trade from its lowest rung upward ("to have risen through the ranks")
column3: raised within the hearth (ocak)
column4: The acemi oğlan recruits taken into the janissary corps trained for years and were then distributed among the companies; even the janissary ağa was most often someone raised within the corps. Because the word ocak was the name for both the family and the army, the expression has been used in both a military and a professional sense. Today it is said of a person who has risen in an institution from apprenticeship to mastery. The word alaylı carries a similar meaning.

column2: great truths cannot be hidden ("you can't hide an elephant under a rug")
column3: a long spear cannot be hidden inside a sack
column4: The spear is a long-shafted weapon of war; even if put into a sack, its tip sticks out. The proverb draws a plain principle from this concrete image: grave crimes and obvious truths cannot be hidden, whatever one does. The saying comes from the eras when the spear was a common weapon in the Ottoman army and is recorded in nineteenth-century dictionaries. Today it is said of secret dealings that come to light.

column2: a person does not harm his own kin or the one who protects him
column3: a sword does not cut its own sheath
column4: The kın is the leather or wooden sheath that protects the sword. However sharp a sword may be, it does not cut its sheath, because the sheath is its own home. The proverb says that a person will not harm his own family or his protector. In Turkish martial culture the sword and sheath together are a symbol of valor. The saying lived in the oral tradition and entered nineteenth-century collections.

column2: everything belongs to the one who knows how to use it and dares to
column3: the horse belongs to the one who rides it, the sword to the one who girds it
column4: In nomadic Turkic society the horse and the sword were the two basic instruments of valor. In the Dede Korkut tales a young man received his name once he rode a horse and girded a sword. The proverb says that the true owner of a thing is the person able to use it. Its structure, an elliptical sentence built on possessive endings, preserves a very old proverb form. Today it is said to stress the importance of ability and courage.

column2: new instruments have swept away the old values of valor and honesty
column3: once the musket was invented, valor was spoiled
column4: The saying is a line attributed to the sixteenth-century folk poet Köroğlu. When firearms spread it became possible to kill by shooting from a distance, and the worth of warriors who fought face to face with the sword declined. Köroğlu is said to have rebelled against this change. The proverb is still used today to say that technological innovations erode old values. The word tüfek is of Persian origin.

column2: to execute by military firing squad
column3: to line up for the bullet
column4: In the age of firearms the military form of capital punishment was for the condemned to be shot by soldiers lined up before a wall. Because condemned prisoners, when more than one, were lined up side by side, the idiom is built with the verb dizmek ("to line up"). This punishment was applied in the late Ottoman period and during the War of Independence. Today the idiom is used literally for historical events and figuratively for a barrage of harsh criticism.

column2: to come into unexpected great fortune ("to have a stroke of luck")
column3: for the bird of fortune to land on one's head
column4: In folktales, when a ruler died the people gathered in the square and a bird was released; whoever's head it landed on was chosen as sultan. This bird was called the devlet kuşu or hüma; the Persian-derived hüma is the legendary bird that brings the throne to whomever its shadow falls on. The word devlet in Arabic carries the senses of both fortune and power. The idiom arose from this folktale motif and came to describe unexpected luck.

column2: to undertake something at the risk of one's life ("to put one's head on the block")
column3: to tuck one's head under one's arm and go
column4: In the Ottoman palace, a vizier who brought bad news to the sultan or opposed him might have his head cut off. For this reason a person embarking on a dangerous task was said to set out with his head under his arm. Kelle, of Persian origin, means head. The idiom was born of this palace reality and today is used for a person who takes on a great danger. The form kelle koltukta ("head under the arm") is also common.

column2: do as you please, the decision is yours ("suit yourself")
column3: as the pasha's heart wishes
column4: Pasha was the title given in the Ottoman state to high officials such as viziers and governors-general. A pasha's wish was not opposed; what he said was done. To tell someone paşa gönlün bilir is to put him in the pasha's place and leave the decision to him; there is a touch of mockery in this usage. The set phrase is one of the traces the palace order left on everyday speech and is still often heard today.

column2: an official loyally bound to the state; a person at the beck and call of a superior
column3: slave of the gate
column4: In the Ottoman state the sultan's palace was called the kapı ("gate"); Bâbıâli, too, means the Sublime Porte. The janissaries and Enderun officials taken into the palace through the devşirme levy took the name kapıkulu because they were bound directly to the sultan. This group drew its salary from the treasury and was distinct from the timar-holding sipahis of the provinces. Today the expression is used for people unconditionally bound to an office or a person.

column2: a private, protected space reserved for its owner alone
column3: the sultan's private garden
column4: The Arabic has means private and select. The gardens around Topkapı Palace belonged to the sultan and were guarded by the bostancıbaşı; these were called has bahçe. The word has was also used in the Ottoman state for the sultan's private revenues. Today the expression is used, often in a critical tone, for a space a person reserves for himself alone or for a privileged place.

column2: a ceremonial phrase declaring loyalty to the ruler ("long live the king")
column3: my sultan, live long
column4: In the Ottoman state, at a sultan's accession, at festival greetings and on return from campaign, soldiers and people shouted padişahım çok yaşa. This phrase was both a prayer and an oath of loyalty. Padişah is formed from the Persian words pâd and şâh. With the Republic the set phrase remained a historical memory; today it is used jokingly to declare loyalty to a superior.

column2: to become ruler; to take the head of an institution ("to ascend the throne")
column3: to sit upon the throne
column4: Taht, of Persian origin, means the ruler's seat. Ottoman sultans began their reign by sitting on the throne set up before the Babüssaade in Topkapı Palace, which was called cülus. Accession gratuities (cülus bahşişi) were distributed to the soldiers and the sword-girding ceremony was held. The idiom passed from the throne ceremony into everyday speech, coming to describe taking the head of an institution or a company.

column2: the command may be yours, but we are free on our own path
column3: the decree is the sultan's, the mountains are ours
column4: The saying is a line from a poem by the nineteenth-century Turkmen bard Dadaloğlu against the Ottoman resettlement policy. When the tribes of the Taurus were to be settled by force, the bard voiced resistance by saying that the decree belonged to the sultan but the mountains remained theirs. Ferman means decree in Persian. Today the saying is used as a formula declaring freedom in the face of authority.

column2: to have a powerful protector who shows favor ("to have friends in high places")
column3: to have a maternal uncle (dayı)
column4: In Anatolia the dayı, the mother's brother, is the person who protects his nephew. In the Ottoman state the beys of janissary origin who governed Algiers and Tunis were also given the title dayı, and their associates benefited from their power. Whether the idiom comes from this title or from the family tie is not certain. Today dayısı olmak means getting things done with a powerful person standing behind one. The form dayısı dümende ("his uncle is at the helm") is also used.

column2: to wait with great respect, hands clasped in front
column3: to stand with hands clasped before the Divan
column4: In the Imperial Council (Divan-ı Hümâyun), viziers and officials stood in the sultan's presence with their hands clasped in front. The Persian pençe means hand and fingers; el pençe is the clasping of the two hands together. Divan durmak means to wait respectfully before the Divan. The idiom passed from palace protocol into everyday speech, coming to describe waiting respectfully before a superior.

column1: ya devlet başa ya kuzgun leşe
column2: either great success is achieved or everything is lost ("all or nothing")
column3: either fortune lands on the head or the raven swarms the corpse
column4: In the Ottoman struggle for the throne among princes, the winner became sultan and the loser was killed. The proverb is the summary of this deadly contest: either the bird of fortune lands on one's head or the corpse is left to the ravens. The kuzgun (raven) is a black crow that feeds on carrion. The saying is the echo of the Ottoman succession order in popular speech and is said today of high-risk ventures.

column2: official institutions, public service
column3: the gate of the state
column4: In the Ottoman state the kapı ("gate") is the place where one enters the service of a notable; the sultan's gate is the state itself. Finding work at the gate of the state meant a secure salary and respectability. The naming of the Bâbıâli with the word for gate also comes from this outlook. The expression continued to be used for civil service in the Republican period. Devlet kapısından ekmek yemek ("to eat bread from the state's gate") means living on a civil servant's salary.

column2: whoever holds the authority is the one whose word counts
column3: whoever holds the seal is Solomon
column4: In Islamic narratives the prophet Solomon ruled over the jinn and the wind by means of the sealed ring on his finger; a jinn who stole the ring took his place for a time. In the Ottoman state the grand vizier's authority also began with the seal given by the sultan; a vizier whose seal was taken back was deemed dismissed. The proverb says that power lies not in the person but in the office. Mühür ("seal") is of Persian origin.

column2: obediently, quietly and without objection ("like a good boy")
column3: like a pasha, like a pasha
column4: The title of pasha was identified in the Ottoman state with dignity and respectability. Children told to behave are told paşa gibi ol ("be like a pasha"), and the reduplicated form describes behavior without objection. In child-directed speech paşa has also been used as a term of endearment for a brave and well-behaved boy. The idiom is an example of a palace title passing into everyday speech with a tone of affection and irony.

column2: a companion who works in the same place and shares the same fate
column3: a comrade serving at the same gate
column4: In the Ottoman state those who served in the household of a vizier or a bey were bound to the same kapı ("gate") and called one another kapı yoldaşı. The janissaries, too, used the word yoldaş for comrades serving in the same company. Yoldaş derives from the Old Turkic word yol ("road"). The expression survives today in the sense of colleague; the workplace sense of the word kapı comes from here.

column2: to cease being loved and valued ("to fall from grace")
column3: to fall from someone's eye
column4: At the palace, being in the sultan's eye meant favor and office; a vizier who fell from his eye was sent into exile or dismissed. In Divan poetry the eye is the measure of the beloved's attention. The idiom passed from this palace reality into everyday speech. In Turkish, göz ("eye") has carried the sense of attention and esteem since the era of the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk; gözüne girmek ("to enter someone's eye") is the idiom with the opposite meaning.

column2: talent develops only if it is appreciated
column3: skill depends on praise
column4: The saying is a line by the nineteenth-century poet Muallim Naci; the continuation of the line says that goods without a buyer go to waste. In the palace and Divan order, an artist's livelihood depended on the favor of his patron; a poet the sultan did not like was forgotten. Marifet is Arabic for knowledge and skill. Today the proverb is used to say that talent needs to be supported.

column1: olmaya devlet cihanda bir nefes sıhhat gibi
column2: nothing in the world is as precious as health
column3: there is no fortune in the world like a single breath of health
column4: The line is from the opening couplet of a ghazal written by Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent under the pen name Muhibbî and has been known since the sixteenth century. Despite all the power he held, the sultan places health above everything. The word devlet here means fortune and happiness. The set phrase is still said often today during visits to the sick and in conversations about health.

column2: to begin spending money freely ("to loosen the purse strings")
column3: to open the mouth of the money purse
column4: Before paper money and wallets became common, akçe and gold coins were carried in leather or cloth purses whose mouth was drawn shut with a cord. The kese was also used in Ottoman finance as the name of a monetary unit worth five hundred kuruş. A person who opens the mouth of his purse is ready to spend. The idiom arose from this concrete gesture and today denotes spending money generously. Kesenin ağzını bağlamak ("to tie the mouth of the purse") has the opposite meaning.

column2: to put an end to a matter; to eliminate someone ("to close the books on")
column3: to roll up and close the account book
column4: In the Ottoman state, merchants and state clerks wrote their accounts on long paper rolls and, when the business was finished, rolled up the scroll and put it away. Defter is of Greek origin and entered Turkish by way of Arabic. Rolling up the register of an account meant closing that account. The idiom passed from this clerical gesture into everyday speech and in time also acquired the meaning of doing away with a person.

column2: to cheat in a transaction, to swindle with an exorbitant price ("to rip off")
column3: to drive a stake into someone
column4: The kazık is a sharp-pointed wooden stake driven into the ground, and it was also used in the Ottoman state as a form of punishment. Cheating a customer in the market and taking too much money was described as driving a stake into him; the comparison conveys the pain felt by the person cheated. The idiom became widespread in nineteenth-century Istanbul slang. Today it survives with derivatives such as kazık yemek ("to get ripped off"), kazıkçı ("swindler") and kazık fiyat ("rip-off price").

column2: very smartly and carefully dressed ("dressed to the nines")
column3: weighing two dirhems and one seed
column4: The dirhem is a small unit of weight used by Ottoman goldsmiths and spice merchants; the çekirdek ("seed") is an even smaller unit based on the carob seed and is the origin of the carat. According to the account, two dirhems and one seed was the exact weight of a gold coin, and a coin of this weight was considered flawless. The phrase was then applied to a person who looks as trim as a flawless coin. The interpretation is undocumented and is passed on as a folk account.

column2: to be worthless, to be of no use
column3: to carry no value in money
column4: Para is a word of Persian origin and in the Ottoman state was the name of a small coin, the subunit of the akçe; forty para made one kuruş. Since the value of goods in the market was measured in money, anything for which no money was given was considered worthless. The idiom arose from this measure. Today it is used to say that an object or a remark is useless; the form beş para etmez ("not worth five para") is more emphatic.

column1: veresiye şarap içen iki kere sarhoş olur
column2: the regret from spending on credit is doubled
column3: one who drinks wine on credit gets drunk twice
column4: Veresiye, derived from the Turkish root vermek ("to give"), means a sale whose payment is deferred. Tavern keepers and grocers kept a credit ledger for familiar customers. The proverb says that wine drunk on credit first makes the head spin and then, on payment day, produces a bewilderment like a second drunkenness. The saying belongs to the Ottoman marketplace idiom, which conveyed the dangers of debt with humor.

column2: to settle accounts; to take revenge ("to settle a score")
column3: to close the account
column4: Hesap, from the Arabic hisab, is the comparison of credits and debts in the ledger at the end of trading in the market. On the return of a caravan or at year's end, merchants settled accounts and the remaining debt was paid. Taken from this commercial transaction, the idiom broadened to mean resolving personal disputes and even taking revenge. The form hesabını görmek ("to settle someone's account") is harsher and used in a tone of threat.

column2: to treat someone as if he no longer exists, to cut off relations ("to write someone off")
column3: to strike someone's name from the account book
column4: Tradesmen entered customers who bought on credit in a ledger; the name of a customer who did not pay his debt or no longer shopped there was struck from the ledger. In Ottoman government offices, too, being struck from the salary and timar registers meant dismissal from office. The idiom arose from this record-keeping procedure and today denotes cutting off relations with a person. The word defter is of Greek origin.

column2: to lose all sense of proportion, to go too far ("to overstep the mark")
column3: to let the weight of the steelyard slip out of place
column4: The kantar, under its Arabic-derived name, is the great scale of the marketplace; weighing is done with a weight called the topuz that slides along its long arm. If the topuz slips to the wrong place the weighing is thrown off and the goods appear short or over. In the Ottoman state, cheating with the kantar was punished by the muhtesip (market inspector). Starting from this error in weighing, the idiom describes losing one's sense of proportion in a matter. The form kantarın topuzunu kaybetmek also exists.

column2: to make the first sale of the day; to do something for the first time
column3: to make the first transaction
column4: The Arabic iftitah means opening; in Turkish it took the form siftah. For a tradesman the first sale of the day is auspicious; the siftah money was touched to the face and to the counter, and a prayer was said. A neighbor would send customers to a tradesman who had not yet made his siftah, which was the marketplace form of Ahi solidarity. Today the expression is also used jokingly for any first experience; siftah bile olmadı means there was not a single sale.

column2: what is bought cheap is also of poor quality ("you get what you pay for")
column3: stew made from cheap meat turns out tasteless
column4: Butchers in the market priced meat according to its quality; because cheap meat was lean and sinewy, its stew was tasteless. Yahni, of Persian origin, is a meat dish cooked with onions. The proverb draws the general rule of shopping from this kitchen observation: the price of cheapness is paid in poor quality. The saying is recorded in nineteenth-century collections and is still often said when shopping today.

column2: a very desolate, remote and lonely place ("the back of beyond")
column3: a place where no bird flies and no caravan passes
column4: Kervan, of Persian origin, is a company of merchants carrying goods on camels. Ottoman trade ran along caravan routes, and caravanserais were built beside these roads. A place no caravan visited meant one far from trade and from life. The idiom doubles the emphasis on desolation by adding that not even a bird flies there. Today it is used for out-of-the-way settlements.

column2: the gaps in a task are filled while the work is under way
column3: the caravan falls into order once on the road
column4: Caravans did not wait for every preparation to be completed before setting out; the order of the camels and the balance of the loads were adjusted on the road, up to the first halting stations. The caravan leader established this order en route. The proverb counsels those who wait for every detail to be arranged in advance to get started. The saying is one of the traces Ottoman caravan trade left on everyday speech and is used often today in the language of entrepreneurship.

column2: to attach no importance at all, to not care ("to not give a damn")
column3: to not give even a metelik
column4: The metelik is a small Ottoman coin worth ten para minted in the nineteenth century; its name is generally accepted to come from the French métallique. Because its value was so low, metelik became the measure of worthlessness in Turkish. To not give a metelik for something is to count it not worth even a metelik. The idiom arose in the same period and gave rise to other idioms such as meteliğe kurşun atmak ("to shoot bullets at a metelik," to be penniless).

column2: having no value whatsoever ("not worth a dime")
column3: not worth even five para
column4: The para was the smallest coin unit in the Ottoman state, one fortieth of a kuruş. Five para was a sum so small it could not buy even a simit. To say in the market that an item was not worth five para was to state that it had no value at all. The idiom arose from this tiny unit and is used today for worthless objects or people. Although the monetary unit has gone, the idiom lives on.

column2: those with capital earn more easily ("money makes money")
column3: money draws money to itself
column4: The merchants of the bedesten did ever larger business as they increased their capital, while small tradesmen stood still. The proverb describes capital attracting profit to itself through the metaphor of a magnet. In Ottoman marketplace language sermaye ("capital") is formed from the Persian words ser and maye. The saying is recorded in nineteenth-century collections and is still said today to describe economic inequality.

column2: a person is as attached to his property as to his life
column3: property is a chip off one's life
column4: A yonga is a small chip pared from wood. The proverb explains attachment to possessions by saying that property is a piece broken off from life itself. In Ottoman commercial society mal, under its Arabic-derived name, meant both goods and wealth. The saying is used both to understand the grief of someone who has lost his property and to censure excessive attachment to it. The word yonga comes from the Turkish root yonmak ("to pare").

column2: to suffer injustice, to be badly harmed ("to get crushed")
column3: to end up under the okka weight
column4: The okka was the basic Ottoman unit of weight and equaled roughly one thousand two hundred eighty grams; okka stones were used on the kantar and on scales. Anything left under a heavy okka stone was crushed. Starting from this image, the idiom describes a person being crushed or suffering injustice. Although the okka was abolished in 1931, the idioms okkalı ("hefty") and okkanın altına gitmek live on.

column2: to lose all one's money and assets ("to go bust")
column3: to load one's capital onto a cat's back
column4: The idiom humorously conveys that the remaining capital has shrunk to no more than a cat could carry; for a merchant who once loaded camels to be reduced to loading his cat means bankruptcy. Sermaye is formed from the Persian words ser and maye. The saying became widespread in the language of nineteenth-century Istanbul tradesmen and is used jokingly today to describe going under in a business.

column2: a person who lives on debt ends up consuming his own assets
column3: one who eats on debt eats from his own purse
column4: A person who bought on credit in the market or borrowed from a moneylender gave all his earnings to the debt when payment day came. The proverb says that debt is a temporary relief and that in the end the purse will be emptied. In the Ottoman state the kese was both a money pouch and the name of a monetary unit worth five hundred kuruş. The saying is recorded in nineteenth-century collections and is still said today as a warning against borrowing.

column2: exactly, to the full; with not a single kuruş short or over ("to the penny")
column3: every kuruş precisely
column4: The kuruş entered Turkish from the name of the European groschen coin and became the basic Ottoman monetary unit from the seventeenth century onward. When an account was closed in the market, the amount due was counted kuruş by kuruş. The idiom describes this exactitude and is used for both payment and calculation. The kuruş, which survived as the subunit of the lira in the Republican period, has kept the idiom alive.

column2: to punish someone by beating the soles of his feet
column3: to tie someone to the falaka and lay him down
column4: The falaka is a pole with a rope passed through both ends; the feet of the person to be punished were tied to this rope and raised, and his soles were beaten with a rod. It was a common punishment used in the Ottoman state in kadi courts, schools and guild discipline. The word is of Arabic origin. The falaka was banned in the late 1800s and disappeared entirely with the Republic. Today the idiom is used figuratively in the sense of harsh punishment.

column2: to end up in court because of a dispute
column3: to become a matter for the court
column4: In the Ottoman state, disputes were first dealt with through family elders and the neighborhood imam, and only if no settlement was reached did the parties go to the kadi's court. Ending up in court was a source of shame for the family and the neighborhood. The idiom reflects this social pressure; mahkemelik olmak still describes an undesirable situation. Mahkeme derives from the Arabic root hüküm ("judgment").

column2: no one can object to a punishment imposed in accordance with the law
column3: the finger cut off by the law does not hurt
column4: In the Ottoman state the law rested on the sharia and the sultan's statutes; one had to submit to the judgment the kadi gave according to these rules. The proverb says that a lawful punishment must be accepted. Cutting off a finger is a softened expression of the punishment of cutting off a hand. In the Republican period the saying has also been spoken with kanun ("law") in place of şeriat. Today it is used for the acceptance of a just punishment.

column2: no office remains anyone's forever
column3: the court is not the kadi's own property
column4: In the Ottoman state kadis were appointed for a fixed term and, when their term ended, gave up their place to another; this arrangement was meant to prevent the kadi from allying with local power. Starting from this practice, the proverb says that office is temporary. Kadı is Arabic for one who gives judgment; mülk means ownership. Today the saying is said to censure ambition for office.

column2: to swear in God's name that a statement is true
column3: to swear an oath in the name of God
column4: In the kadi's court, when there was no evidence, the parties were asked to swear; yemin, of Arabic origin, passed from the sense of right hand to that of oath. Billah is Arabic for in the name of God. In court the oath sworn on the Quran determined the outcome of the case. The idiom passed from this procedure into everyday speech and is used today to reinforce the truth of a statement. The form vallahi billahi comes from the same source.

column2: having a record of crime or misconduct in one's past ("with a bad record")
column3: whose register is not clean
column4: Sicil, of Arabic origin, means a register. Ottoman kadis recorded every case in registers called şer'iyye sicilleri, and a person's past cases could be found in these registers. A person who had previously committed a crime was considered to have a bad record, and his testimony was not accepted. The idiom arose from this system of records and today is used for a person's past in both judicial and professional life.

column2: to catch someone in the act of committing a crime ("to catch red-handed")
column3: to catch on top of the crime
