column4: In Ottoman law a witness was needed to prove a crime; the culprit being caught during the act was considered the strongest evidence. Suçüstü is a Turkish compound meaning on top of the crime and describes this situation. The subaşı and the night watchmen (asesler) drew up a suçüstü report when catching a criminal at night. Today the idiom is used both in legal language and in everyday life for catching someone at an embarrassing moment.

column2: to make a place or a life unbearable ("to make a living hell of")
column3: to turn into a dungeon
column4: Zindan, of Persian origin, is the dark prison beneath fortresses and palaces. In the Ottoman state debtors and criminals were held in the dungeon while awaiting judgment; because of its damp and dark conditions the dungeon became the measure of unbearableness. The idiom is used in the sense of turning a home or a life into a dungeon. The form dünyayı zindan etmek ("to make the world a dungeon") is also common.

column2: a person sentenced to a heavy penalty; someone who works at very hard labor ("a galley slave")
column3: a person condemned to the oar
column4: In the Ottoman state, to find oarsmen for the galleys, serious criminals were sentenced to the oar and chained to the rowing bench. This punishment was applied from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century and in the galleon era turned from rowing into arsenal labor. Even after the oar sentence was abolished, heavy imprisonment was called kürek. Today the expression is used figuratively for harsh working conditions.

column2: to execute by hanging
column3: to hang with a rope
column4: In the Ottoman state the death penalty varied with the culprit and his status; ordinary criminals were hanged, while state officials were strangled or beheaded. Execution by hanging was carried out before the public in the market square. İpe çekmek describes the condemned being hauled up by the rope. Today the idiom is used literally for historical events and figuratively for severe punishment. İpe gitmek ("to go to the rope") comes from the same root.

column2: for justice to be done, for everyone to receive what he deserves
column3: for the right to reach its proper place
column4: The Arabic hak means both rightness and what is owed. The purpose of the kadi's court was defined as the right reaching its owner; when judgment was given, the right was deemed to have found its place. The idiom denotes the realization of justice and is most often said when a long-standing injustice is finally put right. In the Kutadgu Bilig, justice is treated as the fundamental pillar of the state.

column2: justice is the foundation of the state and of order
column3: justice is the foundation of the realm
column4: The saying is the Turkish translation of an Arabic legal maxim; mülk here means the state and sovereignty. The Kutadgu Bilig relates that justice holds up the ruler's power, and Ottoman political treatises treat the same principle under the name of the circle of justice. In the Republican period the set phrase was inscribed on the walls of courtrooms. Adalet comes from the Arabic root adl.

column2: beating is a necessary instrument of discipline ("spare the rod and spoil the child")
column3: the beating stick came out of paradise
column4: In the Ottoman understanding of education and punishment, beating was a common method both at school and in court; the falaka was its institutionalized form. The proverb legitimized this practice by tracing beating to a sacred source. Dayak comes from the Turkish root dayamak ("to prop") and originally meant a supporting stick. Today the saying is a trace of an old approach to discipline that is mostly criticized, and it is cited in an ironic tone.

column1: kırk katır mı kırk satır mı
column2: to be forced to choose between two bad options ("between the devil and the deep blue sea")
column3: to be torn apart by forty mules or chopped up with forty cleavers
column4: In folktales and popular stories, a person found guilty is made to choose between two forms of execution: being tied to forty mules and torn apart, or being chopped up with forty cleavers. A satır is a butcher's cleaver. The idiom arose from this folktale motif and describes situations in which both options are bad. The number forty is the number for multitude in Turkish folktales. Today the idiom is used jokingly for hard choices.

column2: to give permission or approval on a matter as an authority
column3: to issue a religious legal opinion
column4: Fetva, of Arabic origin, is the written opinion a mufti gives on a legal question. In the Ottoman state the şeyhülislam issued fetvas on many matters, from the sultan's decisions to declarations of war, and the kadi relied on fetvas when giving judgment. The idiom passed from this official procedure into everyday speech, coming to describe a superior giving permission for something. Fetva almak means to obtain permission.

column2: to hold someone captive by binding him in chains; to restrict his freedom
column3: to bind with a chain
column4: In Ottoman dungeons and in the oar sentence, chains were fastened to prisoners' feet and captives were chained to one another. Zincir ("chain") is a word of Persian origin. The verb vurmak here describes hammering the iron shut; prangaya vurmak ("to put in fetters") has the same structure. Beyond actual captivity, the idiom is used figuratively to describe binding the freedom of a person or an idea.

column2: an enmity sustained between families to avenge a murdered relative ("blood feud")
column3: a case for blood
column4: The blood feud is the avenging of a killed person by his family in societies where customary law comes before state law. Ottoman kadis tried to resolve these cases through the rules of blood money (diyet) and retaliation (kısas) and intervened to make peace between families. The expression is a remnant of the ancient Turkic customary law also traceable in the Dede Korkut tales. Today it is used in legal language and in social debate.

column2: to deceive by hiding the truth, to fool with show ("to pull the wool over someone's eyes")
column3: to paint the eye
column4: In the workshops of painters and tinsmiths, old or defective goods were covered with glossy paint and sold as new; in the market this trick was called göz boyamak. Some hold that the idiom comes from conjurers deceiving the spectator's eye. Both accounts describe covering the truth with show. The idiom is recorded in nineteenth-century dictionaries and today is used for work done merely for appearance.

column2: to lose control of a matter, to lose one's sense of proportion ("to lose the thread")
column3: to let go of the end of the thread in one's hand
column4: On the weaving loom and in the carpet workshop, when the end of the thread was lost the whole order of the knots was thrown off and the worker could not find where to continue. For a child flying a kite, too, losing the end of the string means everything slipping away. The idiom arose from these concrete situations and describes losing control of a task or of one's behavior. İp ("thread, rope") is a word used since Old Turkic; the form ipin ucu kaçmak also exists.

column2: to do a very hard and long task patiently and with inadequate tools
column3: to dig a well using a needle
column4: Digging a well is heavy work requiring pick and shovel; doing it with a needle is next to impossible. The idiom presents this impossibility as an example of patience. It is akin to patience motifs in folk stories, such as Ferhat tunneling through the mountain. The needle, the tool of tailors' and embroiderers' workshops, was chosen as the smallest of implements. Today the idiom is said of long-drawn-out and exhausting tasks.

column2: to secretly prepare a trick or a trap; to set up a business ("to set someone up")
column3: to set up a weaving or market stall (tezgâh)
column4: Tezgâh, of Persian origin, is the common name for the frame on which a weaver weaves cloth and the table on which a tradesman sells his goods. Setting up a weaving loom, in the sense of arranging the threads beforehand, demands long preparation. This preparation turned into a metaphor for a secret plan; in nineteenth-century slang tezgâh acquired the meaning of a trick. Today the idiom describes both setting up a business and scheming.

column2: to be able to make a living under any conditions, to be highly resourceful
column3: to get bread out of stone
column4: Craftsmen such as stonemasons, millers and wall-builders earn their living from stone; the millstone turns wheat into bread. The idiom makes drawing a livelihood even from a substance as barren as stone the measure of resourcefulness. Ekmek ("bread") is the Turkish name for a livelihood. The saying is recorded in nineteenth-century dictionaries and today is said in praise of hardworking, resourceful people.

column2: work made by hand with great care and labor ("a labor of love")
column3: the labor of the hand and the light of the eye
column4: Craftsmen doing fine work, such as calligraphers, miniaturists, carpet weavers and goldsmiths, wore out their eyes over the years; göz nuru dökmek means to pour the light of one's eyes into a work. Nur is Arabic for light. By joining the labor of the hand with the light of the eye, the expression conveys how carefully a product has been made. Today it is used for handmade products and for work that demands effort.

column2: every task should be done when its time comes and conditions are right ("strike while the iron is hot")
column3: iron is forged while it is hot
column4: The smith hammers on the anvil the iron he has heated in the forge before its heat passes; cooled iron does not take shape and cracks. Tav in Turkish means the heated state fit for working. The proverb turns this smith's knowledge into the principle of seizing an opportunity in time. The saying is a universal observation with equivalents in European languages, and in Turkish it is framed in the language of the smithy.

column2: to be squeezed between the pressure of two powerful parties ("between a rock and a hard place")
column3: to be crushed between the anvil and the hammer
column4: In the smithy the hot iron is placed on the anvil and beaten with the hammer; anything that comes between anvil and hammer is crushed. Örs ("anvil") is a word used since Old Turkic. From this concrete image the idiom describes the condition of a person caught between two pressures. The same metaphor exists in many languages. Today it is often said of people caught in the middle in politics and in business.

column2: to ruin someone's business, to turn his order upside down ("to throw a wrench in the works")
column3: to recite a spell over the wheel
column4: Çark, of Persian origin, is the wheel turned by the knife grinder, the potter and the miller; a workshop's operation depends on the wheel turning. According to the account, reciting over the wheel means casting a spell on it to stop it turning. The idiom arose from this folk belief and came to describe ruining someone's business. This slangy saying has the same structure as the idiom canına okumak ("to recite over someone's life," to finish someone off).

column2: to vouch with absolute certainty for the truth of something ("to stake one's reputation on")
column3: to stamp one's seal or mold on it
column4: In foundry and mold-making workshops the product comes out of the master's mold; the mold carries both the shape and the master's signature. Textile printers, too, printed their designs with wooden blocks, and the block owner's name became a stamp on the goods. Kalıbını basmak is to vouch for the truth of something as if it were one's own product. Kalıp ("mold") is of Arabic origin. Today the idiom is used to give a firm guarantee.

column2: a task cannot be done that quickly and easily ("it's not that simple")
column3: is this a dyer's vat, that it should come out at once?
column4: The dyer dips the cloth into the dye vat and pulls it out; the job is done in a few minutes. But other jobs do not finish so fast. The idiom is a reply to hasty demands: Boyacı küpü mü, daldırıp çıkarasın ("Is it a dyer's vat, that you dip it in and pull it out?"). Boya ("dye") and küp ("vat") are words used since Old Turkic. The saying is one of the traces that the dye-houses of the Ottoman marketplace left on everyday speech and is said today to convey that a job takes time.
